```{r Q5, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=6, fig.width=10, results='show', cache=FALSE}
#### Q5: per-gene linear model age ~ expression, CI of the slope with confint() ####

# One gene: fit the model, return slope, its 95% CI (confint), and p-value
gene_ci <- function(expression, age) {
  tryCatch({
    fit <- lm(age ~ expression)
    ci  <- confint(fit, "expression", level = 0.95)
    co  <- summary(fit)$coefficients
    c(estimate = co["expression", "Estimate"],
      lower    = ci[1, 1],
      upper    = ci[1, 2],
      p.value  = co["expression", "Pr(>|t|)"])
  }, error = function(e) c(estimate = NA, lower = NA, upper = NA, p.value = NA))
}

# Debug on the first 100 genes
test_ci <- t(sapply(1:100, function(i) gene_ci(exprNorm[i, ], age)))
head(test_ci)

# Full run over all probes (takes a few minutes)
system.time(
  ci.mat5 <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(exprNorm)),
                      function(i) gene_ci(exprNorm[i, ], age),
                      numeric(4)))
)
rownames(ci.mat5) <- rownames(exprNorm)

ci.tbl <- data.frame(probe    = rownames(ci.mat5),
                     SYMBOL   = Dat$SYMBOL[match(rownames(ci.mat5), Dat$ID)],
                     ci.mat5,
                     width    = ci.mat5[, "upper"] - ci.mat5[, "lower"],
                     sd.expr  = apply(exprNorm, 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE),
                     row.names = NULL)
cat("Models that could not be fitted:", sum(is.na(ci.tbl$p.value)), "\n")
ci.tbl <- ci.tbl[!is.na(ci.tbl$p.value), ]

#### Order genes by strength of relationship (p-value, smallest first) ####
ci.tbl <- ci.tbl[order(ci.tbl$p.value), ]
ci.tbl$rank <- seq_len(nrow(ci.tbl))
excl.zero   <- ci.tbl$lower > 0 | ci.tbl$upper < 0     # CI does not contain 0
cat("CIs excluding zero:", sum(excl.zero), "of", nrow(ci.tbl), "\n")

#### Plot 1: CI for every gene, in p-value order ####
{
  ylim.clip <- quantile(c(ci.tbl$lower, ci.tbl$upper), c(0.01, 0.99))   # clip extreme widths
  graphics::plot(range(ci.tbl$rank), ylim.clip, type = "n",
                 xlab = "Genes ranked by p-value (strongest -> weakest)",
                 ylab = "95% CI of slope (years per unit expression)",
                 main = "95% confidence intervals of the expression coefficient, all genes\n(age ~ expression, GSE11882, quantile normalized)",
                 sub  = "y-axis clipped at the 1st-99th percentile of CI bounds")
  graphics::segments(ci.tbl$rank, ci.tbl$lower, ci.tbl$rank, ci.tbl$upper,
                     col = ifelse(excl.zero, rgb(0.8, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3), rgb(0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 0.3)))
  graphics::abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  graphics::legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.85, lwd = 2,
                   legend = c("CI excludes 0", "CI includes 0"),
                   col = c(rgb(0.8, 0.1, 0.1), "grey40"))
}

#### Plot 2: zoom on the 50 strongest and the 50 weakest genes ####
{
  op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  for (part in c("strong", "weak")) {
    idx <- if (part == "strong") 1:50 else (nrow(ci.tbl) - 49):nrow(ci.tbl)
    d   <- ci.tbl[idx, ]
    graphics::plot(d$rank, d$estimate, pch = 19, cex = 0.6,
                   ylim = range(c(d$lower, d$upper, 0)),
                   xlab = "Rank by p-value", ylab = "Slope and 95% CI (years per unit)",
                   main = if (part == "strong") "50 strongest genes" else "50 weakest genes")
    graphics::segments(d$rank, d$lower, d$rank, d$upper,
                       col = ifelse(d$lower > 0 | d$upper < 0, "firebrick", "grey40"))
    graphics::abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  }
  graphics::par(op)
}

#### Strongest and weakest gene: report their CIs ####
extreme5 <- ci.tbl[c(1, nrow(ci.tbl)), ]
extreme5$case <- c("Strongest", "Weakest")
knitr::kable(extreme5[, c("case", "probe", "SYMBOL", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
                          "width", "p.value", "sd.expr")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "95% CI of the expression coefficient (age ~ expression)")

#### Plot 3: the two genes' data with fitted line and 95% confidence band ####
{
  op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  for (j in 1:2) {
    pid <- extreme5$probe[j]
    d   <- data.frame(age = age, expression = exprNorm[pid, ])
    fit <- lm(age ~ expression, d)
    gx  <- data.frame(expression = seq(min(d$expression), max(d$expression), length.out = 100))
    pr  <- predict(fit, gx, interval = "confidence")
    graphics::plot(age ~ expression, d, pch = 19, col = "grey50",
                   main = paste0(extreme5$case[j], ": ", extreme5$SYMBOL[j], " (", pid, ")"),
                   xlab = "Expression (quantile normalized)", ylab = "Age (years)")
    graphics::polygon(c(gx$expression, rev(gx$expression)), c(pr[, "lwr"], rev(pr[, "upr"])),
                      col = rgb(0.8, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2), border = NA)
    graphics::lines(gx$expression, pr[, "fit"], col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
  }
  graphics::par(op)
}
```

**Results.** 17,604 of the 44,134 probe intervals (40%) exclude zero, far more than the roughly 2,200 (5%) expected by chance; this is the same count as the p < 0.05 genes after normalization in Week 3. The strongest relationship is **CX3CL1** (823_at): slope −25.8 years per unit of expression, 95% CI [−30.6, −21.0], width 9.6. The weakest is **SRSF3** (232392_at): slope 0.0, 95% CI [−7.4, 7.4], width 14.9, p = 1.

**Interpretation.** *Position* shows direction and whether "no effect" is plausible. CX3CL1's whole interval lies well below zero, so every plausible value says higher expression goes with younger donors, and zero is firmly ruled out. SRSF3's interval is centred exactly on zero, so its data are equally consistent with a positive, negative or no relationship, and its estimated slope means nothing. *Width* shows precision. The slope's standard error is about σ_residual / (SD of expression × √(n − 1)). The two genes have similar expression spread (SD 0.62 vs 0.51), so SRSF3's wider interval comes from its larger residual error: its expression explains none of the variation in age, so the residuals keep the full spread of age (SD ≈ 25 years), while CX3CL1 explains about 40% of it. CX3CL1's interval is narrow relative to its distance from zero, so we can trust both its sign and its approximate size: roughly 21–31 years per unit of expression. Raw widths are not directly comparable between genes in general, because each slope is in units of that gene's own expression. Two caveats apply. With 44,134 tests, about 2,200 intervals would exclude zero by chance alone, so the strongest genes are convincing because their intervals lie far from zero, not just outside it. And as in Week 3, GSE11882 contains several brain regions per donor, so the samples are not independent; the model treats 173 samples as independent, which makes every interval narrower than it should be.


### Question 6

Time series analysis of a real repeated-measures clinical signal.

Query a table from the course’s DuckDB/Parquet repository (Week 1 Part 3) that contains a repeated measurement on the same patient or subject over time, for example a vital sign or lab value recorded at multiple time points in MIMIC-III. Use DBI::dbListTables()/DESCRIBE to confirm the table’s structure before proceeding. Following the approach developed in Week 4 Part 4:

**a.**: Construct a time-ordered series for one patient, or one subject, with enough repeated measurements to be meaningful, and use STL decomposition to separate the series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components. If your chosen series has no plausible periodic component, decompose it into trend and remainder only, and explain why you left out a seasonal term.

```{r Q6a, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=8, fig.width=10, results='show', cache=FALSE}

library(DBI)
library(duckdb)

#### 1. Get MIMIC-III demo CHARTEVENTS (same PhysioNet source as the course repository) ####
# The quick repoquet repository has no repeated-measurement table, and its build
# fails (UCI #891 download), so CHARTEVENTS is downloaded once into data/mimic_demo.
mimic_dir <- file.path("data", "mimic_demo")
dir.create(mimic_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ce_file <- file.path(mimic_dir, "CHARTEVENTS.csv")
ce_done <- paste0(ce_file, ".complete")       # marker written only after a complete download
ce_url  <- "https://physionet.org/files/mimiciii-demo/1.4/CHARTEVENTS.csv?download="

if (!file.exists(ce_done)) {
  if (!requireNamespace("curl", quietly = TRUE) || packageVersion("curl") < "5.0.0") install.packages("curl")
  for (k in 1:10) {                           # retry and RESUME interrupted downloads
    res <- tryCatch(curl::multi_download(ce_url, ce_file, resume = TRUE, progress = TRUE),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(res) && isTRUE(res$success)) { file.create(ce_done); break }
    message("Attempt ", k, " incomplete (", round(file.size(ce_file) / 1e6, 1),
            " MB so far); resuming...")
    Sys.sleep(3)
  }
  stopifnot(file.exists(ce_done))
}

#### 2. Load into DuckDB and confirm the table structure (Week 1 Part 3) ####
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
dbExecute(con, sprintf(
  "CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE chartevents AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('%s', header = true, auto_detect = true, sample_size = -1)",
  ce_file))
dbListTables(con)                                        # "chartevents"
print(dbGetQuery(con, "DESCRIBE chartevents"))           # column names and types
print(dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT subject_id) AS n_patients,
                              COUNT(DISTINCT icustay_id) AS n_icu_stays FROM chartevents"))

#### 3. Choose one ICU stay: most heart-rate readings, spanning at least 3 days ####
# Heart rate item IDs: 211 (CareVue) and 220045 (MetaVision); 20-250 bpm drops artefacts
stays <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT icustay_id, subject_id, COUNT(*) AS n_hr,
         MIN(charttime) AS first_time, MAX(charttime) AS last_time,
         date_diff('hour', MIN(charttime), MAX(charttime)) AS span_hours
  FROM chartevents
  WHERE itemid IN (211, 220045) AND valuenum BETWEEN 20 AND 250 AND icustay_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY icustay_id, subject_id
  ORDER BY n_hr DESC
  LIMIT 10")
print(stays)
chosen.stay <- stays$icustay_id[stays$span_hours >= 72][1]   # need >= 3 full 24-h cycles
stopifnot(!is.na(chosen.stay))
chosen.subj <- stays$subject_id[stays$icustay_id == chosen.stay]
cat("Chosen ICU stay:", chosen.stay, "| subject:", chosen.subj, "\n")

hr.raw <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT charttime, valuenum AS hr
  FROM chartevents
  WHERE icustay_id = %d AND itemid IN (211, 220045) AND valuenum BETWEEN 20 AND 250
  ORDER BY charttime", as.integer(chosen.stay)))
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)            # data is now in R's memory

#### 4. Regular hourly series (STL needs equally spaced, gap-free data) ####
t0 <- as.POSIXct(trunc(min(hr.raw$charttime), "hours"))
hr.raw$hour <- floor(as.numeric(difftime(hr.raw$charttime, t0, units = "hours")))
hourly <- aggregate(hr ~ hour, data = hr.raw, FUN = mean)          # mean within each hour
grid   <- data.frame(hour = 0:max(hourly$hour))
grid$hr <- approx(hourly$hour, hourly$hr, xout = grid$hour, rule = 2)$y   # fill gaps
pct.imputed <- 100 * mean(!grid$hour %in% hourly$hour)
grid$clock.hour <- (as.numeric(format(t0, "%H", tz = "UTC")) + grid$hour) %% 24

cat("Raw readings:", nrow(hr.raw), "| hourly points:", nrow(grid),
    "| days:", round(nrow(grid) / 24, 1),
    "| hours interpolated:", round(pct.imputed, 1), "%\n")

hr.ts <- ts(grid$hr, frequency = 24)          # one "season" = 24 hours

#### 5. STL decomposition: trend + 24-hour seasonal + remainder ####
stl.fit <- stl(hr.ts, s.window = "periodic", robust = TRUE)   # robust: ICU spikes
comp <- stl.fit$time.series
Tt <- comp[, "trend"]; St <- comp[, "seasonal"]; Rt <- comp[, "remainder"]

# Strength of trend and seasonality (0 = none, 1 = dominant)
strength <- c(trend    = max(0, 1 - var(Rt) / var(Tt + Rt)),
              seasonal = max(0, 1 - var(Rt) / var(St + Rt)))
round(strength, 3)
c(seasonal.amplitude.bpm = round(diff(range(St)), 1),
  trend.range.bpm        = round(diff(range(Tt)), 1),
  remainder.sd.bpm       = round(sd(Rt), 2))

#### 6. Plots (each wrapped in { } so its pieces always run together) ####
# (i) raw readings and hourly series
{
  graphics::plot(as.numeric(difftime(hr.raw$charttime, t0, units = "hours")) / 24, hr.raw$hr,
                 pch = 20, cex = 0.5, col = "grey60",
                 xlab = "Days since first reading", ylab = "Heart rate (bpm)",
                 main = paste0("Heart rate, ICU stay ", chosen.stay, " (subject ", chosen.subj, ")"))
  graphics::lines(grid$hour / 24, grid$hr, col = "steelblue", lwd = 1.5)
  graphics::legend("topright", bty = "n", legend = c("Charted readings", "Hourly series"),
                   pch = c(20, NA), lty = c(NA, 1), col = c("grey60", "steelblue"), lwd = c(NA, 1.5))
}

# (ii) STL decomposition
{
  plot(stl.fit, main = "STL decomposition: heart rate = trend + 24-h seasonal + remainder")
}

# (iii) the 24-hour pattern by clock hour, and the ACF of the detrended series
{
  op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
  daily <- tapply(as.numeric(St), grid$clock.hour, mean)
  graphics::plot(as.numeric(names(daily)), daily, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "firebrick",
                 xlab = "Clock hour", ylab = "Seasonal component (bpm)",
                 main = "Estimated 24-hour pattern", xaxt = "n")
  graphics::axis(1, at = seq(0, 23, 3))
  graphics::abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  stats::acf(as.numeric(hr.ts - Tt), lag.max = 72, main = "ACF of detrended series (lags in hours)")
  graphics::abline(v = c(24, 48, 72), col = "firebrick", lty = 3)
  graphics::par(op)
}

#### 7. Trend + remainder only (used if the 24-h component turns out negligible) ####
if (strength["seasonal"] < 0.2) {
  lo  <- loess(hr ~ hour, data = grid, span = min(1, 48 / nrow(grid)))   # ~2-day smoother
  Tt2 <- predict(lo); Rt2 <- grid$hr - Tt2
  cat("Trend + remainder only: trend range =", round(diff(range(Tt2)), 1),
      "bpm | remainder SD =", round(sd(Rt2), 2), "bpm\n")
  {
    op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
    graphics::plot(grid$hour / 24, grid$hr, type = "l", col = "grey50", xlab = "Days", ylab = "bpm",
                   main = "Trend + remainder only (no seasonal term)")
    graphics::lines(grid$hour / 24, Tt2, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
    graphics::plot(grid$hour / 24, Rt2, type = "l", col = "steelblue",
                   xlab = "Days", ylab = "Remainder (bpm)")
    graphics::abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
    graphics::par(op)
  }
}
```

**b**: Test the series for stationarity with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test (adf.test()). If it is non-stationary, apply first-differencing and re-test. Explain, in terms of this specific series, what stationarity means and why it matters before fitting an ARIMA model.

```{r Q6b, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=6, fig.width=10, results='show', cache=FALSE}

#### Q6b: stationarity (Augmented Dickey-Fuller test) ####
if (!requireNamespace("tseries", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("tseries")
library(tseries)

# H0: the series has a unit root (non-stationary)
adf.raw <- adf.test(hr.ts)
adf.raw

# If non-stationary (p >= 0.05): first-difference and re-test
hr.use <- hr.ts
if (adf.raw$p.value >= 0.05) {
  hr.use   <- diff(hr.ts)                    # hour-to-hour change in heart rate
  adf.diff <- adf.test(hr.use)
  print(adf.diff)
}

# Plot the original and the differenced series
{
  op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  graphics::plot(hr.ts, col = "grey40", xlab = "Days", ylab = "bpm",
                 main = paste("Heart rate (ADF p =", signif(adf.raw$p.value, 3), ")"))
  graphics::plot(diff(hr.ts), col = "steelblue", xlab = "Days", ylab = "Change (bpm/hour)",
                 main = "First-differenced heart rate")
  graphics::abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  graphics::par(op)
}
```

**c**: Fit an ARIMA model to the series (differenced, if needed) using auto.arima(), and forecast the next several time points with prediction intervals. Plot the forecast and interpret it in plain language: does the forecast look clinically plausible given the trend and variability you observed in part (a)?

```{r Q6c, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=6, fig.width=10, results='show', cache=FALSE}

#### Q6c: ARIMA fit and forecast ####
if (!requireNamespace("forecast", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("forecast")
library(forecast)

# Differencing order from part (b): 1 if the ADF test said non-stationary, else 0
d.use <- ifelse(adf.raw$p.value >= 0.05, 1, 0)

# Fit ARIMA (no seasonal term: the 24-h component was negligible in part a)
arima.fit <- auto.arima(hr.ts, d = d.use, seasonal = FALSE)
summary(arima.fit)

# Residual check: Ljung-Box p > 0.05 means no autocorrelation left
checkresiduals(arima.fit)

# Forecast the next 24 hours with 80% and 95% prediction intervals
hr.fc <- forecast(arima.fit, h = 24, level = c(80, 95))
print(round(data.frame(hour     = 1:24,
                       forecast = as.numeric(hr.fc$mean),
                       lo95     = as.numeric(hr.fc$lower[, "95%"]),
                       hi95     = as.numeric(hr.fc$upper[, "95%"]))[c(1, 6, 12, 24), ], 1))

# Plot: last 5 days of data + 24-hour forecast
{
  graphics::plot(hr.fc, xlim = c(max(time(hr.ts)) - 5, max(time(hr.ts)) + 1),
                 xlab = "Days", ylab = "Heart rate (bpm)",
                 main = "24-hour heart rate forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals")
}
```


#### Interpretation

**Data and series (part a).** The course's quick repoquet repository has no repeated-measurement table (its MIMIC-III demo tables are admissions, diagnoses, ICU stays, patients and procedures), and its build currently fails because of an unrelated download error. We therefore downloaded `CHARTEVENTS`, the bedside vital-signs table, from the same open-access MIMIC-III demo on PhysioNet, loaded it into DuckDB and confirmed its structure with `dbListTables()` and `DESCRIBE`: 758,355 charted measurements for 99 patients and 133 ICU stays, one row per measurement (`subject_id`, `icustay_id`, `itemid`, `charttime`, `valuenum`, …). Heart rate (item IDs 211 and 220045, restricted to 20–250 bpm) was extracted for the ICU stay with the most readings, ICU stay 249805 (subject 10126): 1,115 readings over 35.2 days. Readings were averaged into hourly bins, and the 2.8% of hours with no reading were filled by linear interpolation, giving a regular series of 845 hourly values.

**Decomposition (part a).** We first ran STL with a 24-hour seasonal term, since heart rate normally follows a circadian rhythm and MIMIC preserves the time of day. The data did not support it. The seasonal strength was only 0.012 (0 = none, 1 = dominant), and the estimated daily cycle had an amplitude of just 2.4 bpm, well below the remainder's SD of 5.8 bpm. The trend, by contrast, was strong (strength 0.795, range 50 bpm). We therefore decomposed the series into **trend and remainder only**, with a LOESS smoother spanning about two days. The trend shows large multi-day swings: heart rate climbs from about 80 to about 120 bpm over the first week, falls to a low of about 67 bpm around day 13, then rises and falls repeatedly between roughly 80 and 123 bpm (peaks near days 23 and 33). This is the pattern we would expect from a long ICU course with episodes of deterioration and recovery. The remainder (SD 4.9 bpm) is centred on zero, with a few isolated spikes (e.g. +35 bpm near day 17, −26 bpm near days 15 and 27) that likely reflect brief clinical events or charting artefacts. A missing circadian rhythm is clinically plausible: critical illness, sedation, continuous lighting and round-the-clock care are known to blunt or abolish the normal day–night pattern, and here the day-to-day changes in the patient's condition are far larger than any daily cycle.

**Stationarity (part b).** A series is stationary when its statistical behaviour (mean, variance and correlation between nearby hours) stays the same over time. For this patient, that means heart rate keeps returning to the same typical level with a similar spread, rather than drifting permanently up or down. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test (null hypothesis: a unit root, i.e. non-stationary) rejected non-stationarity (ADF = __, p = __), so the series was treated as stationary and **no differencing was needed** (d = 0). This fits the plot: despite large excursions, heart rate repeatedly comes back to roughly 95–100 bpm instead of wandering off. Stationarity matters before fitting an ARIMA model because ARIMA assumes the relationship between each hour and the preceding hours is the same throughout the series. If the mean drifted (a non-stationary series), the model would mistake that drift for short-term dependence, and its coefficients, standard errors and forecasts would be unreliable. Differencing would then be needed to model hour-to-hour *changes* instead. The test result comes with a caveat. The fitted AR coefficients sum to about 0.98, very close to 1, so this series is only just stationary: deviations from the mean fade very slowly, which is exactly why the trend shows long multi-day swings.

**ARIMA model and forecast (part c).** `auto.arima()` selected an **ARIMA(4,0,1)** model with a mean of 97.4 bpm. Each hour's heart rate depends on the previous four hours plus a short-term error correction. The residual standard deviation (√22.78 ≈ 4.8 bpm) matches the remainder from part (a), and the Ljung-Box test found no autocorrelation left in the residuals (Q* = 37.8, df = 43, p = 0.70), so the model captured the series' time structure adequately. The 24-hour forecast starts at 95.5 bpm, close to the last observed values, and drifts only slightly, to 96.0 bpm, slowly pulled toward the long-run mean of 97.4 bpm. The prediction intervals widen quickly: the 95% interval is 86–105 bpm one hour ahead, 79–111 bpm at 6 hours, and 74–118 bpm at 24 hours.

**Is the forecast clinically plausible?** Broadly, yes. The forecast level (about 95 bpm) sits in the patient's typical range, at the upper end of normal and close to the 100 bpm threshold for tachycardia, consistent with an ICU patient. The 24-hour interval (74–118 bpm) spans almost exactly the range seen over the final five days (about 75–127 bpm). Short-term forecasts are the most informative: within the next few hours, heart rate is very likely to stay close to its current level. Beyond that, the forecast mostly says "somewhere in this patient's usual range," and the widening intervals honestly reflect that uncertainty. The model also has clear limits. It projects past patterns forward and knows nothing about why heart rate changes, so it cannot anticipate abrupt events like the rise from about 92 to 127 bpm within a few hours around day 34 (driven by something clinical such as fever, pain, bleeding or a change in medication). An observation like that could fall outside even the 95% interval. An ARIMA forecast like this is therefore useful as a baseline for flagging unexpected values, rather than as a prediction of the patient's clinical course.
